q: In a stack navigator, which screen does the user see?
options: The last route in the list, the top of the stack
The first route in the list
All routes at the same time
The route with the longest name
why: A stack is a list of routes. The last one is on top, and that is the screen you see. Going back removes it, and the one under it shows again.

q: You are on the Details screen and call navigate('Details', { id: 8 }). A second Details screen is added to the stack.
why: No. The React Navigation docs say navigate only pushes if you are not already on that route. If you are on Details, nothing changes. Use push to add a second Details screen.

q: The stack starts as Home. You call push('A'), then push('B'), then popToTop(). Put the stacks in the order they appear after each call.
why: push A gives Home, A. push B gives Home, A, B. popToTop removes everything except the first route, so only Home is left.

q: Which of these are good things to put in route params?
options: A big object with the whole product
why: The docs recommend params that are JSON-serializable and small. A big object goes stale, and a function cannot be saved or put in a deep link.

q: Which route.params property would the Details screen read after navigation.navigate('Details', { productId: 7 })? Type the full expression, for example route.params.name.
why: Params go in the second argument and the screen reads them from route.params.

q: You open a Post in the Home tab, switch to the Profile tab, then switch back. With the default settings, what do you see?
options: The Post, because each tab keeps its own stack
The first screen of the Home tab, always
why: Each tab can keep its own stack. The tab option popToTopOnBlur resets a nested stack when you leave the tab, and its default is false.
